Thursday, 11 April. Hélène has had a fever since this morning. Julien talks in the corridor with Dr Martin, the care home doctor, four days before the laying of the foundation stone.
Doctor, how is she? She looked so well last Wednesday.
She has a temperature of thirty-eight point five. It’s not very serious, but at her age we have to be careful. She has to stay in bed until the fever goes down.
And Monday? She absolutely wants to attend the laying of the foundation stone in La Duchère.
I know. She’s told me ten times since this morning. But I can’t promise anything. I have to examine her before she goes out.
What can we do in the meantime?
Until she feels better, she has to drink a lot and sleep. And above all, not get worked up.
(smiles) Not get worked up? You don’t know her very well. Since she found out she might not be able to come, she’s furious.
I’d noticed. She called me "Doctor Tyrant". (laughs) Right. As soon as the fever has gone down, I’ll examine her. If she’s stable on Sunday evening, she can go out on Monday.
One hour, no more. In a wheelchair, well wrapped up, and someone will have to stay with her until she’s back.
Odile will stay with her. She hasn’t left her side since yesterday. She reads her books while she rests.
That’s very good. A retired paediatrician makes a good nurse. But she needs to sleep too. I found her asleep in the armchair this morning.
I’ll tell her to go home tonight. I’ll stay until Hélène falls asleep.
All right. And before you leave, come by my office. I’ll give you my number, in case there’s a problem during the night.

"Avant que" (before) takes the SUBJUNCTIVE, because the action hasn’t happened yet. An expletive "ne" (with no negative meaning) often appears in careful language:
Je dois l’examiner avant qu’elle (ne) sorte.
Passez à mon bureau avant de partir.
Don’t put "pas" after the expletive "ne": "avant qu’elle ne sorte" = before she goes out (not "before she doesn’t go out").
2. Jusqu’à ce que, en attendant que + subjunctive
Both express a time limit ("until") and take the SUBJUNCTIVE:
I’ll stay until Hélène falls asleep.
Until she feels better, she has to sleep.
"Jusqu’à ce que" stresses the limit (up to that moment, no longer). "En attendant que" stresses what you do in the meantime. Without a verb: "jusqu’à lundi", "en attendant lundi".
3. Après que, pendant que, dès que + indicative
Conjunctions expressing a real fact (simultaneous or earlier) take the INDICATIVE:
Elle lit pendant qu’elle se repose.
Dès que la fièvre aura baissé, je l’examinerai.
Depuis qu’elle sait, elle est furieuse.
Après qu’elle est partie, il a pleuré.

The classic mistake (made even by French people): "après qu’elle soit partie". The rule: after "après que" you use the INDICATIVE: "après qu’elle EST partie". The logic: once something has happened, it’s a real fact. Simpler still: "après son départ" or "après être partie".
quand, lorsque, dès que, pendant que, depuis que, après que
avant que, jusqu’à ce que, en attendant que
Memory trick: the ones looking towards a FUTURE moment not yet reached ("before", "until") take the subjunctive. The ones describing something that is happening or has happened take the indicative.
"Comment va-t-elle ?" = How is she? "Elle va mieux" = She’s better. The verb "aller" is the one used for health, not "se sentir" (which is more specific: "je me sens fatigué").

On Thursday 11 April, at seven in the morning, Julien’s phone rang. It was Madame Lambert, sounding worried. Hélène had woken up with a fever. Nothing serious, the night nurse had said, but she preferred to let the family know before the doctor arrived. Julien took the first funicular.

When he came into the room, Hélène was sitting up in bed, her cheeks red, her eyes shining with fever and anger. Odile was already there, on a chair next to the bed, a book open on her knees. She looked as if she hadn’t slept. She hadn’t.

"They want to stop me going on Monday," said Hélène before Julien had even said hello. "I heard them in the corridor. They say I have to stay in bed until the fever goes down. And what if it doesn’t? I’ve waited sixty-seven years to see a music room in Henri’s name. I’m not waiting one more week."

Julien sat on the edge of the bed and took her hand. It was burning. "The doctor said she’d examine you on Sunday evening," he explained gently. "If the fever has gone down, you’ll be able to come. One hour. In the meantime, you need to sleep. And not get worked up."

"I’m not getting worked up," Hélène replied in a furious voice. "I’m perfectly calm." Odile looked up from her book, Julien looked at Odile, and all three of them burst out laughing at the same time. Hélène laughed until a coughing fit made her stop. Then she sank back onto her pillows, exhausted.

That same day, in La Duchère, the site was being prepared. A digger had dug the foundations, and workers were putting up fences around the plot. Radu came by every day to check on progress, with Chloé and the safety binder. But that Thursday he had another mission, a far more important one: finding the lime tree.

He had called every nursery in the region. Most offered him young lime trees, two or three metres tall, delivered by lorry. But Radu wanted something special. He didn’t know exactly what. He only knew he couldn’t plant just any tree in front of Hélène’s room.

It was Odile who had given him the idea, without meaning to. One evening, talking about the 1962 photo, she had said: "The bench was in the Parc de la Tête d’Or, near the lake. Henri showed it to me once, without telling me why. There was a huge lime tree behind it. I wonder if it’s still there."

On Friday morning, before going to the office, Radu went to the Parc de la Tête d’Or with the photo. He walked around the lake for an hour, comparing every bench and every tree with the old black-and-white picture. The joggers gave him strange looks. A gardener eventually asked him what he was looking for.

Radu showed him the photo. The gardener, an elderly man with a grey beard, looked at it for a long time. Then he smiled. "The bench has been gone for a long time," he said. "But the lime tree is still here. Come." He led him to a corner of the park, by the water, where a huge tree stood, its trunk as wide as a car.

"It’s over a hundred and fifty years old," the gardener explained. "It’s the oldest lime tree in the park. Lovers used to come and sit under it in the old days. There was a bench here until they replaced it with a path, back in the eighties." Radu looked up at the branches, still bare, where the first buds were appearing.

He told the gardener the whole story: Hélène, Henri, the waltz, the La Duchère room, the lime tree he had promised. The old man listened without interrupting. At the end, he scratched his beard. "You can’t transplant it, obviously. But wait. I may have something for you."

He took him to the park’s greenhouses, behind the rose garden. There, in a corner, lined up in pots, were about a dozen young trees a metre and a half tall. "These are its children," said the gardener. "Ten years ago, I gathered seeds from under the old lime tree and grew them. For the day it falls."

Radu didn’t know what to say. He looked at the young lime trees, then at the gardener, then at the trees again. "Would you give me one?" he finally asked. The gardener smiled. "I can’t give it to you. It belongs to the city. But I can lend it for a municipal project. And a music room for children is a municipal project, isn’t it?"

He chose the straightest, sturdiest tree himself. He promised to deliver it to La Duchère on Monday morning, before the ceremony began. Radu shook his hand for at least a minute. As he left, he turned back towards the old lime tree by the lake. For a moment, he thought he could hear a waltz being whistled.

Meanwhile, at Fourvière, Odile never left Hélène’s side. She stayed with her day and night, until Julien or Ioana came to take over. She read her novels, poems, the newspaper. In the evening, Hélène always asked her the same thing before falling asleep: to read her Henri’s letter again, the one from 1963.

Odile read it slowly, in a low voice. She almost knew it by heart now. It was a short, clumsy letter, written by a wounded young man who didn’t dare come back. A letter that had never been sent. Hélène listened with her eyes closed, and when Odile reached the last sentence, she murmured it with her.

On Saturday, the fever began to go down. Thirty-eight, then thirty-seven point eight. Hélène ate a little soup and asked for news of the lime tree. When Julien told her about the gardener and the old tree in the Tête d’Or, she said nothing for a long time. Then she asked: "Is it still there? The big one?"

Julien nodded. Hélène closed her eyes. "Henri kissed me for the first time under that tree," she murmured. "On 3 May 1962. He carved our initials into the bark, on the lake side. Maybe the gardener has seen them." She fell asleep before Julien could reply, a smile at the corner of her lips.

That same evening, Radu went back to the park with a torch. He went round the old lime tree three times, lighting up the bark centimetre by centimetre. He was about to give up when he saw them, very high up, almost worn away by time and weather: two letters intertwined inside a heart. An H. And another H.

He stood motionless, torch in hand, until the park keeper came to tell him the gates were closing. He took a photo with his phone. On the screen the letters were barely visible. But they were there. Henri and Hélène. For sixty-seven years.

On Sunday, early, a surprise arrived at the care home. Yanis and Inès, with Madame Mansouri, brought a big envelope. Inside were thirty-six drawings, one from each child in the orchestra. Violins, lime trees, musical notes, and lots of elderly ladies in enormous hats.

On every drawing, the children had written the same sentence, copied from the school board with lots of spelling mistakes: "Get well soon, Madame Hélène, we’re waiting for you on Monday." Hélène asked for them all to be put up on the wall opposite her bed, so she could see them as soon as she opened her eyes. Madame Lambert spent an hour putting them up, without correcting a single mistake.

Yanis came up to the bed, very shy. He had brought his cello in its black leather case. "The doctor said you couldn’t go out," he said. "So I came to play here. Just a little. Until you get tired." Hélène smiled and signalled to him to begin.

He played his solo, the one from the regional council, sitting on a chair at the foot of the bed. The sixteen bars filled the little room. In the corridor, residents came out of their rooms to listen, in dressing gowns and slippers. When he finished, Hélène had fallen asleep, her hand resting on Yanis’s drawing, a huge lime tree under a sky full of stars.

On Sunday morning, the fever was down to thirty-seven point two. Dr Martin came by at eleven. She examined Hélène at length, in silence, under the anxious eyes of Odile and Julien. Then she put away her stethoscope and said with a sigh: "One hour. Not a minute more. And I’m coming with you."

Hélène took her hand. "Thank you, doctor," she said. "Sorry about the tyrant." The doctor smiled. "You know, in twenty years of practice, it’s the first time a patient has called me a tyrant because I want to look after her. And the first time I’ve gone to a foundation-stone ceremony with an eighty-six-year-old patient."

In the evening, Radu came with Lucia, Ioana and Rose-Hélène. He showed Hélène the photo of the initials on his phone, zooming in as far as it would go. Hélène looked at the screen through her magnifying glass for a very long time. Her hands were shaking. She didn’t cry. She only said, very softly: "He carved them. I never knew if he really had."

Then she asked Julien for one last thing. She wanted to go down to the Salle Henri Bernard, just for five minutes, to hear the two waltzes. Dr Martin had said "no going out", but she hadn’t said anything about the lift. Madame Lambert pretended not to see them go by in the corridor.

The room was empty and dark. Julien switched on a single lamp, above the piano. He played Henri’s waltz, then, without stopping, his own, as on the evening of 15 July. Hélène listened from her wheelchair, Rose-Hélène asleep on her lap, wrapped in a blanket. Odile held Hélène’s hand.

When the last note faded, nobody moved. Outside, the city was slowly lighting up. Hélène stroked the hair of the little girl asleep against her. Then she said, in a clear, almost cheerful voice: "Tomorrow, the foundation stone. And the lime tree. The old tree’s children. Henri would have loved that." She smiled. "I love it too."

That evening, Odile finally went home to sleep in her own bed. Before leaving, she put the 1963 letter on Hélène’s bedside table, next to the photo, the score and the little sprig of orange blossom, now dry. Hélène was already asleep. She was breathing calmly, regularly, like someone who has nothing left to wait for, and everything to hope for.
